t: Introduction: physical factors and aim of the session
n: This chapter covers four groups of physical factors: high and low temperature, electric current, pressure changes and radiation. The effect of low temperature occurs in almost all cases as a result of an accident. Electrical injury accounts for 1–2.5% of all injuries. However, it holds one of the leading places among causes of disability and death. In a corpse found after a fire, it is necessary to establish whether the action of flame was vital, that is, whether it occurred before or after death.

t: Body temperature and routes of heat loss
n: Body temperature and routes of heat loss. Normal body temperature is 36–37 °C; heat production and heat loss are regulated. Of heat loss, radiation accounts for 55%, sweat for 27%, conduction for 15%, and various secretions for 3%. If the temperature is below 22–25 °C or above 43–44 °C, the tissues change in a way incompatible with life. General action is heat stroke or general cooling, and local action is a burn or frostbite.

t: Heat stroke: causes and mechanism of development
n: Heat stroke: causes and mechanism of development. The cause is that a lot of heat is produced and little is lost: high temperature and humidity, lack of wind, heavy work. Predisposing conditions: clothing impermeable to air, cardiovascular disease, obesity and old age. The sequence of the mechanism is as follows. First heat accumulates, then the blood thickens and circulation slows, after which hyperthermia and hypoxia develop. Then stress appears, catecholamines and stasis are observed, and metabolism is disturbed. Haemodynamic disturbance occupies the leading place.

t: Acute and protracted forms of heat stroke
n: Acute and protracted forms of heat stroke. In the acute form, in an unacclimatised organism, consciousness is suddenly lost, coma develops and death occurs in a short time. In the protracted form the signs build up slowly; the central nervous system is first depressed. The periods follow one another: a period of depression, that is, the latent period, then a period of excitation, then a period of exhaustion, in which the temperature is above 41–42 °C. Then comes the preagonal state: coma and convulsions. If the body temperature exceeds 42–43 °C, death occurs from primary respiratory arrest.

t: Sunstroke and changes in the corpse
n: Sunstroke and changes in the corpse. In the corpse the brain and meninges are congested and swollen; small perivascular haemorrhages are found in the brain tissue. The internal organs are congested, the blood in the heart and large vessels is thick, and the lungs are brownish. Rigor mortis develops quickly and strongly, while cadaveric lividity appears late and is scanty. Let us compare heat stroke and sunstroke. In heat stroke much heat is produced and little is lost, the temperature may exceed 41–42 °C, and the changes in the corpse are similar. In sunstroke sunlight acts on the head for a long time, a considerable rise in temperature is not characteristic, and headache, hallucinations and convulsions occur. There is no specific feature.

t: Quick questions: heat stroke and sunstroke
n: Quick questions on heat stroke and sunstroke. How many periods are there in the protracted form of heat stroke? Three: depression, excitation and exhaustion. Which factors predispose to heat stroke? High temperature and humidity, lack of wind, heavy work, clothing impermeable to air, obesity, old age, cardiovascular disease. Is there a special morphological sign in the corpse characteristic of heat stroke or sunstroke? No, the changes are similar and non-specific. Attention: heat stroke is not sunstroke. In heat stroke the whole body overheats; in sunstroke the head is heated by the rays; the temperature does not rise considerably.

t: Thermal burns: sources and four degrees
n: Thermal burns: sources and four degrees. Cause: flame, flammable substances, water hotter than 60 °C, steam, gas or a heated object. In first degree there are erythema, slight swelling and pain; it resolves without trace in 3–4 days and is often not visible in the corpse. In second degree, blisters with serous fluid form and heal without scarring in 10–20 days; the base of the blister is brown and firm, and no blood emerges on incision. In third degree there is necrosis: III-A superficial, III-B full thickness; granulation and a scar form in 2–3 weeks. In fourth degree there is necrosis of skin, muscle, ligament and bone. Burns of the first to third degree may come from any source, whereas the fourth degree arises only from flame.

t: Determining the source of a burn
n: Determining the source of a burn. Streaks run toward the lower parts of the body, while "tongues of flame" run toward the upper parts. This direction helps assess the position of the victim at the time of the event. Differences between sources: with hot liquid, the hair and clothing are not damaged, the injury is superficial and streak-like, and the liquid also runs into covered areas. With flame, the hair and clothing are damaged, the injury is deep and tongue-shaped, and there are traces of soot. With a heated object, the injury is deep and limited, corresponding to the shape of contact. With steam and hot gas, burns of the airways are characteristic. Attention: burns of the airways are given as an injury characteristic only of the action of steam and hot gas.

t: Burn area and severity criteria
n: Burn area and severity criteria. The rule of the palm: a person's palm makes up about 1% of the body surface. The diagnosis is written as a fraction: the area in the numerator, the degree in the denominator. For example: 30% (10%) / II–III. The burn areas dangerous to life are as follows: for third to fourth degree, more than 10%; for third degree, more than 15%; for second degree, more than 20% of the surface. With burn disease or airway oedema, even a smaller area may be life-threatening.

t: Four periods of burn disease
n: Four periods of burn disease. The first period is burn shock, lasting up to 1 day. The second period is toxaemia, 1–2 weeks. The third period is septicotoxaemia, 2–3 weeks to a month. The fourth period is convalescence, that is, recovery. If airway burns and carbon monoxide are added, the likelihood of death in shock increases two-fold or more. In septicotoxaemia, pneumonia, abscess, phlegmon, pyelonephritis, sepsis and cachexia, that is, extreme emaciation, are observed. In young children and the elderly, burn disease is more severe.

t: Establishing the vitality of flame action
n: Establishing the vitality of flame action. If soot is found in the airways, oesophagus and stomach, the flame acted during life. Soot is also found in the frontal sinus, in vessels, in leukocytes and in the Kupffer cells of the liver. Carboxyhaemoglobin reaches 60% during life, and after death does not exceed 20%. Carboxymyoglobin is found in the deep muscles. In the "crow's feet" sign, the bottom of the eyelid folds is free of soot: the eyeballs are usually not damaged, and when the eyelid skin is stretched, burnt and unburnt areas alternate. Arterial thrombi, pulmonary fat embolism and a two-fold excess of protein in blisters are also signs of vitality.

t: Case analysis: a corpse found after a fire
n: Case analysis: a corpse found after a fire. Situation: after a fire the body is completely charred and was found in the "pugilistic attitude", with the arms and legs flexed. The posture arises from evaporation of moisture, coagulation of protein and shortening of the muscles. An epidural haematoma was found inside the skull. Question: did the flame act before death or after it? Which signs and samples will you examine? Death in a fire most often results from carbon monoxide poisoning, while the corpse is charred after death.

t: Case analysis: a corpse found after a fire (continued)
n: We continue this case analysis. Therefore a microscopic examination of the skin and internal organs is necessary. Attention: an epidural haematoma from trauma is spindle-shaped and adherent to the dura mater. One produced by the action of flame after death is crescent-shaped and not adherent. By this difference the two can be distinguished.

t: Low temperature: factors and stages of general cooling
n: Low temperature: factors and stages of general cooling. Humidity, wind, inappropriate clothing, fatigue and intoxication predispose to general cooling. Infants are particularly sensitive, because thermoregulation is not fully formed and the body surface is relatively large. In cold water death occurs in 1–1.5 hours; with sudden immersion it may also be due to vascular collapse or shock. The stages: first compensation, in which the temperature rises; then decompensation, in which the temperature falls. At +30…+28 °C cortical function is disturbed; at +25…+22 °C the terminal stage begins.

t: External signs of general cooling on the corpse
n: External signs of general cooling on the corpse. In the posture of a frozen person, the arms are flexed toward the chest and the legs toward the abdomen. Rayski's signs: ice in the mouth and nose, hoarfrost on the eyebrows and eyelashes. In Puparev's sign, the testicles are retracted and the scrotum is raised. Cadaveric lividity at a positive temperature, down to +10 °C, is bluish-violet; at a negative temperature it is pinkish-red, because the blood contains a lot of oxygen. Attention: an ice crust beneath the snow is non-specific; it also forms on a corpse that has not yet cooled. In severe intoxication the "posture of a frozen person" may be absent.

t: Internal signs of general cooling
n: Internal signs of general cooling. Because of the increased permeability of the vessel wall, diapedetic haemorrhages are found in the internal organs. The organs are congested and the tissues pink. In the left heart and aorta the blood is clotted and bright scarlet. Innervation is disturbed, smooth muscles are paralysed and the urinary bladder is full of urine. In Pukhnarevich's sign the stomach is empty and considerably reduced in size. In Fabrikantov's sign, small haemorrhages are found in the renal pelvis. Wischnewski spots, that is haemorrhages in the gastric mucosa, occur in 80–90% of cases; in rapid death they are few or absent.

t: Wischnewski spots: sign and mechanism
n: Wischnewski spots: sign and mechanism. In the mucosa of the stomach, and sometimes of the duodenum, there are small haemorrhages up to 0.5 cm in diameter. They occur in 80–90% of those who died of general cooling and may be detectable even 6–9 months after death. Sequence of the mechanism: the action of low temperature, autonomic nervous disturbance, vascular spasm and diapedesis, haemorrhagic infarction, and finally Wischnewski spots. In rapid death the spots are few or absent, and in children they are often not observed; in slow death they are numerous.

t: Microscopy, histochemistry and the frozen corpse
n: Microscopy, histochemistry and the frozen corpse. On microscopy, proliferation and necrobiotic changes of the epithelium of the straight renal tubules are found; this is Kasyanov's sign. Glycogen disappears in the liver, pancreas, heart and brain, and lipoids in the adrenal cortex. In very rapid death sugar decreases, while glycogen in the liver may be preserved. In severe intoxication under the effect of cold, alcohol in the blood may be low and in the urine high; the cause is intensive utilisation of alcohol.

t: Microscopy, histochemistry and the frozen corpse (continued)
n: We continue with the frozen corpse. In a corpse frozen at sub-zero temperature, small cracks appear, and freezing of the brain may fracture the skull bones. Rapid thawing increases haemolysis and imbibition.

t: Frostbite: degrees and features
n: Frostbite: degrees and features. The latent period is the time of cooling; the reactive period begins after warming, and the degree is distinguished by depth. In first degree the skin is reddish-bluish and swollen, resolving in 3–7 days. In second degree there are blisters with clear fluid, healing without scarring in 10–20 days. In third degree there are skin necrosis and a haemorrhagic blister, healing with a scar in 1–2 months. In fourth degree there is necrosis of tissue and bone. Repercussion: when frostbite affects one side, changes may also develop in the opposite arm or leg. Frostbite of the third to fourth degree over more than 10% of the surface, of the third degree over more than 15%, and of the second degree over more than 20% is dangerous to life.

t: Case analysis: general cooling and frostbite
n: Case analysis: general cooling and frostbite. Situation: the corpse of an intoxicated person was found in the open air, with the arms flexed toward the chest and the legs toward the abdomen. Which signs confirm the vital action of low temperature? The flexed "posture of a frozen person" indicates vital action; in severe intoxication the posture may be absent, so its absence does not exclude the action. Small haemorrhages up to 0.5 cm in the gastric mucosa, Wischnewski spots, occur in 80–90% of cases; if death is rapid, they may be few or absent. In severe intoxication under the effect of cold, alcohol in the blood may be low and in the urine high. The cause is the body's intensive utilisation of alcohol.

t: Electrical injury: features and current factors
n: Electrical injury: features and current factors. Although electrical injury accounts for 1–2.5% of all injuries, it holds a leading place in disability and mortality. Current cannot be detected without a special instrument; it may act by contact, indirectly or at a distance. Even with a brief exposure, a disproportion is observed between the extent and the severity of the injury. Current factors: safe voltage is 24 V; most deaths occur at 220–380 V. The dangerous current is 50 mA, and the most often fatal current is 100 mA. The especially dangerous frequency is 40–60 hertz.

t: Organism factors and tissue resistance
n: Organism factors and tissue resistance. Children, the elderly and pregnant women are more sensitive. Diseases of the heart, nervous system and respiratory organs, hypoxia, intoxication and heat stroke lower the body's resistance. The "attention factor": expecting current leads to caution, and when shocked, to rapid disconnection from the source. This explains why electrical injury is less common in electricians. The order of increasing resistance: blood, mucous membrane, liver, kidney, muscle, brain, lung, ligament, cartilage, nerve, bone, skin.

t: Organism factors and tissue resistance (continued)
n: We continue with this topic. Morphological changes occur mainly in bone and skin. Moist skin and sweating increase the danger, which is why deaths are more frequent in summer. Rubber, leather and silk have high resistance; damp clothing and metal ornaments reduce resistance.

t: Current loop and step voltage
n: Current loop and step voltage. It is dangerous if the current passes through the heart and brain: the upper, left, left oblique and left full loops. With bipolar or earthed contact the current spreads; isolated unipolar contact is usually safe. Step voltage is the potential difference between two points 0.8 m apart; do not approach the place where a broken wire has fallen closer than 10 m. The chain is as follows: the broken wire falls to the ground, an electric crater forms on the ground, and the potential differs between the feet. As a result, leg convulsion occurs, that is the lower loop, then a fall, and the danger of the full loop arises.

t: Specific and non-specific action of electric current
n: Specific and non-specific action of electric current. In general action the electrical processes of cells are disturbed: ventricular fibrillation, respiratory disturbance, shock. There are four types of action. In chemical action, ionic balance is disturbed; the anode is coagulative and the cathode colliquative. In thermal action, current is converted into heat and a burn occurs; in bone, calcium phosphate melts and solidifies, forming hollow white spheres 1–5 mm across, "pearl beads". In mechanical action, skeletal muscle convulsions, joint dislocations and bone fractures are observed. In non-specific action the energy is outside the body: ignition of clothing, burns of the eyes. Impregnation of the skin with metal particles is a chemical action; mechanical action is more common at high voltage.

t: Electrical mark and metallisation
n: Electrical mark and metallisation. The electrical mark forms at the point of entry and exit of the current; it is round or oval, firm, with a raised edge and a crater-like centre. On microscopy, cavities are seen in the horny and clear layers, the cells appear broom-like, and metal particles appear in nests. On thin or moist skin the mark does not form; this may occur in 10–20% of electrical injuries. In metallisation, the colour of the mark depends on the metal: copper, sky-blue, green, yellowish-brown; iron, yellow, brown, black; aluminium, grey, yellowish-brown; lead, grey, dark.

t: Electrical burn and types of death
n: Electrical burn and types of death. An electrical burn is painless and there is no inflammation around it, because the sensory nerve endings are destroyed. The true extent becomes clear in 2–3 weeks; thereafter secondary bleeding from vessel erosion is possible. Apparent death, that is vita minima, is common: if there are no reliable signs, resuscitation is carried out. According to Avdeev there are four types of death. The first is ultra-rapid: immediate arrest. The second is slow: signs of life are present. The third is interrupted: death after the person has come round. The fourth is late: after hours to a day.

t: Lightning strike
n: Lightning strike. The damaging factors of lightning are electric current, light, sound and the blast wave. It acts directly or indirectly, for example through a telephone, television or radio. A red or pink tree-like "lightning figure" appears on the skin: vessels dilate and small haemorrhages occur. The sign is unstable, disappearing within hours to a day, so it is photographed immediately. There are burns and damage on the clothing. Sometimes the outer clothing is intact while the underclothing or body is damaged; metal parts and coins may melt. In survivors the figure may persist for several days, and symmetrical paresis and paralysis may develop. Sometimes there is no injury at all on the body or clothing.

t: Case analysis: electrical injury and lightning
n: Case analysis: electrical injury and lightning. Situation: a corpse was found at home in damp conditions. On the palm there is a round, firm patch with a raised edge and a deep centre; the surrounding skin is unchanged. This corresponds to an electrical mark. Metallisation gives the mark its colour: from a copper conductor, bluish-green; from iron, yellow-black. The imprint of the metal colour is determined by X-ray and emission spectrography. Moist skin creates favourable conditions for the current. If there is no reliable sign of death, apparent death is possible: resuscitation is carried out until cadaveric lividity appears. Question: why is the lightning figure photographed immediately? Answer: it is an unstable sign and disappears after a few hours, sometimes after a day.

t: High pressure: barotrauma and lung injury
n: High pressure: barotrauma and lung injury. Under water, hydrostatic pressure is added to atmospheric pressure: at 10 m the pressure increases 2-fold, at 20 m 3-fold. When ascending with an aqualung, holding the breath at a depth of 10 m sharply raises the pressure inside the lungs. If the pressure changes abruptly by 80–100 mm Hg, pulmonary barotrauma develops, that is, an injury related to pressure. The chain: pressure changes abruptly, the bronchi and alveoli rupture, air passes into the capillaries, and arterial air embolism occurs. In the corpse under water, bubbles are observed.

t: Compression in divers and gas poisoning
n: Compression in divers and gas poisoning. Compression of the body is characteristic of divers: if the diving suit is faulty, blood rushes to the head and the face turns blue. At a carbon dioxide level of 3% or more, shortness of breath, weakness, headache and sweating are observed. Nitrogen dissolves in fat 5 times better than in blood; in the brain, euphoria resembling intoxication appears. There are two forms of oxygen poisoning. In the neurotoxic form the pressure is 2.5–3.0 and higher, for a short time; the main damage is in the brain: loss of consciousness, convulsions. In the pulmonary form the pressure is 1.0–1.5, for more than 2 hours or repeatedly; the main damage is burning of the lungs and pneumonia. Pressure is measured in megapascals. In both forms there are no specific changes in the corpse.

t: Decompression sickness and low pressure
n: Decompression sickness and low pressure. On rapid ascent, the nitrogen in blood and tissue is released, and bubbles of free gas block the blood vessels. The chain: rapid ascent from depth, pressure falls abruptly, nitrogen turns into gas bubbles, and decompression sickness, that is caisson disease, develops. In the corpse, gas bubbles are found in the blood: gas clots in the right heart and veins, subcutaneous emphysema, foamy fluid in the liver. Altitude sickness is oxygen deficiency; at 6 kilopascals, that is at 18,000 m, tissue fluid "boils".

t: Case analysis: pressure change
n: Case analysis: pressure change. Situation: a diver with an aqualung is rising to the surface and holds his breath at a depth of 10 m. In this case the volume of air in the lungs increases and the pressure inside the lungs rises sharply. As a result pulmonary barotrauma occurs. If the lung ruptures, air passes into a blood vessel. Air embolism of the cerebral arteries is considered the most dangerous. In the corpse, the vessels of the heart and lungs are ligated and the organs placed in water, and air is introduced into the lungs. Bubbles emerge from the site of rupture.

t: Radiation: mechanism of action and dose forms
n: Radiation: mechanism of action and dose forms. Neutron, gamma and X-rays penetrate deeply. Alpha and beta particles have low penetrating power and are stopped by clothing. Ionising radiation causes radiolysis of water and DNA damage; cell division is suppressed. The most sensitive are the bone marrow, skin, intestine and gonads. Dose and form: bone marrow form up to 10 grays, intestinal form 10–20, toxaemic form 20–80, cerebral form above 80. The bone marrow form above 6 grays leads to death.

t: Acute radiation sickness and changes in the corpse
n: Acute radiation sickness and changes in the corpse. First comes the primary reaction, 3–4 days: nausea, vomiting, weakness. Then the latent period, 2–4 weeks; the hair begins to fall out. Then the marked clinical period follows. Complications: bleeding and infection. Death occurs at the end of the 4th week. If death occurs in the marked period, the corpse shows multiple haemorrhages and destructive changes in the bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen. Gonads: the scrotum shrinks, and in the ovary the follicles atrophy.

t: Chronic and local radiation injury and expert examination
n: Chronic and local radiation injury and expert examination. Chronic radiation sickness develops with repeated action of small doses: haemopoiesis is disturbed and bleeding increases; death is most often from infection. Radiation burns resemble thermal burns; neutron, gamma and X-rays also damage muscles, bones and internal organs. Radiation ulcers heal slowly, with a risk of suppuration and tumour. The tasks of the expert examination: the type of damaging factor, the physical characteristics of the source, the dose, how many times and when the exposure occurred, and the degree of severity of the bodily injury. To resolve these, the circumstances of the event, working conditions, the properties of the source, dispensary records, radiometry and the macroscopic and microscopic examination of the corpse are used.

t: Case analysis: death related to irradiation
n: Case analysis: death related to irradiation. In situation A, death occurs in the first hours after irradiation. In the corpse, only signs characteristic of rapid death are expected, and changes characteristic of radiation sickness are not yet present. In situation B, death occurs during the period of marked clinical signs. Multiple haemorrhages, destruction in the bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen, pneumonia, peritonitis and sepsis are expected. Dose and form: up to 10 grays bone marrow, 10–20 intestinal, 20–80 toxaemic, above 80 cerebral form. The bone marrow form above 6 grays leads to death.

t: Case analysis: death related to irradiation (continued)
n: We continue the case analysis. Question: when is death expected after a single dose of 50 Gy, and above 150 Gy? Answer: at 50 Gy, usually within the first two days; above 150 Gy, immediately, from paralysis of the brain centres.

t: Conclusion: key points of the expert examination of physical factors
n: Conclusion: key points of the expert examination of physical factors. When flame has acted during life, there is soot in the airways, oesophagus and stomach. Attention: carboxyhaemoglobin is also found after death, but does not exceed 20%; during life, up to 60%. In general cooling, the "posture of a frozen person" and Wischnewski spots are characteristic. Attention: in rapid death the spots are few or absent, and in children they are often absent. In electrical injury, an electrical mark forms at the point of entry and exit of the current; in apparent death, resuscitation is carried out.

t: Conclusion: key points of the expert examination of physical factors (continued)
n: We continue the conclusion. The "lightning figure" disappears quickly, so it is photographed immediately. In pulmonary barotrauma, finding air embolism in the vessels of the lungs, heart and brain confirms it. The severity of radiation injury depends first of all on the dose.
